title: What are common replication topologies — single-primary + read replicas, multi-primary/active-active (conflict resolution needed), cascading replication (replica feeds another replica) — and when do you use each?
shortTitle: Common replication topologies and when to use each

s1_definition.profdef: A replication topology is the arrangement of which nodes replicate to which. Single-primary with read replicas sends all writes to one primary and fans reads out to replicas. Multi-primary (active-active) accepts writes on more than one node, which requires conflict detection and resolution. Cascading replication has a replica forward changes to downstream replicas, reducing load on the primary.
s1_definition.analogy: Single-primary is one head office that records every change and mails copies to branches for reading. Multi-primary is several branches all allowed to write at once — powerful but risky, because two branches might change Rajesh's record differently and you must reconcile. Cascading is a regional hub that receives from head office and relays to its own sub-branches, so head office is not overwhelmed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Single-primary for most apps (simple, read scaling); multi-primary only when you truly need multi-region writes (and accept conflict resolution); cascading to offload fan-out from the primary.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A replication topology is the arrangement of which nodes replicate to which. Single-primary with read replicas sends all writes to one primary and fans reads out to replicas. Multi-primary (active-active) accepts writes on more than one node, which requires conflict detection and resolution. Cascading replication has a replica forward changes to downstream replicas, reducing load on the primary.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Single-primary is one head office that records every change and mails copies to branches for reading. Multi-primary is several branches all allowed to write at once — powerful but risky, because two branches might change Rajesh's record differently and you must reconcile. Cascading is a regional hub that receives from head office and relays to its own sub-branches, so head office is not overwhelmed.

**One line to remember:** Single-primary for most apps (simple, read scaling); multi-primary only when you truly need multi-region writes (and accept conflict resolution); cascading to offload fan-out from the primary.

sections.s2_technical:
Single-primary with read replicas is the default: one writable primary, several read-only replicas. Writes are simple and consistent; reads scale horizontally; replicas serve reporting and can be promoted on failover. The limits are replica lag (read-your-writes needs care) and a single write bottleneck.

Multi-primary/active-active lets multiple nodes accept writes, useful for low-latency writes across regions or continuous availability. The hard part is conflict resolution when two nodes modify the same row — strategies include last-write-wins by timestamp, per-column merge, or application-level reconciliation. Banks avoid active-active for the core ledger because money cannot tolerate conflicting writes; they prefer partitioning writes by region or using a single-writer design.

Cascading replication has a replica act as an upstream for further replicas, forming a tree. This reduces WAL fan-out pressure on the primary when there are many replicas or cross-region hops. The cost is extra lag per hop and a more complex failover path.

Senior nuance: choose by write pattern and consistency need. Most systems start single-primary and add read replicas; cascade when replica count or geography strains the primary; adopt multi-primary only when multi-region write availability is a hard requirement and the data model tolerates conflicts.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India has one writable ledger, many reporting readers, and a far region whose replicas should not hammer the primary. This maps to single-primary plus read replicas with a cascading hop, while the core ledger deliberately stays single-writer to avoid conflicts.

The demo has a `TopologyRouter` that routes writes to the primary, reads to replicas, and models a cascading replica that feeds a downstream replica, plus a conflict check illustrating why active-active is risky for the ledger.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__topology_note.sql
-- Single-primary + read replicas: app routes writes to primary, reads to replicas.
-- Cascading: replica_mumbai streams from replica_delhi, not from the primary.
-- Multi-primary: requires conflict handling — AVOID for the ledger.
CREATE TABLE ledger (
    account_id VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    balance    DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    version    BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0   -- optimistic version for conflict detection
);
INSERT INTO ledger VALUES ('SAV2001', 1000000.00, 0), ('CUR3001', 250000.00, 0);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
topology:
  primary: db-primary-delhi          # all writes
  read-replicas: [replica-delhi, replica-mumbai]
  cascade:
    replica-mumbai:
      upstream: replica-delhi        # cascading: feeds from replica, not primary
  ledger-writes: single-primary-only # no active-active for money
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: one primary (Delhi), two replicas (Delhi, and Mumbai cascading from Delhi), a write and two reads, plus a simulated active-active conflict.

Step 1: routeWrite sends Rajesh's balance update to the single writable primary — all writes converge there.

Step 2: routeRead round-robins: the first read hits replica-delhi, the second hits replica-mumbai, which is noted as cascaded from replica-delhi rather than the primary.

Step 3: detectConflict shows two primaries both writing version 5 would clash, illustrating why the ledger stays single-writer.

```text
2026-10-25 18:32:00 [INFO] WRITE -> db-primary-delhi
2026-10-25 18:32:00 [INFO] READ -> replica-delhi
2026-10-25 18:32:00 [INFO] READ -> replica-mumbai (cascaded from replica-delhi)
2026-10-25 18:32:00 [SEVERE] CONFLICT: two primaries wrote version 5 — needs resolution
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  WRITES ─────────────→ db-primary-delhi  (single writer)
                             │ streaming WAL
                 ┌───────────┴───────────┐
                 ▼                        ▼
           replica-delhi ──cascade──→ replica-mumbai
                 ▲                        ▲
               READS (round-robin, reporting / far region)

  (active-active alternative: 2 writers → version clash → conflict resolution)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The three common replication topologies are single-primary with read replicas, multi-primary or active-active, and cascading replication. Single-primary sends all writes to one writable node and fans reads out to read-only replicas, which keeps writes simple and consistent while scaling reads and giving failover candidates; its limits are replica lag and the single write bottleneck. Multi-primary accepts writes on more than one node for multi-region write availability, but it demands conflict detection and resolution — last-write-wins, per-column merge, or application reconciliation — because two nodes can change the same row differently. Cascading replication lets a replica forward changes to downstream replicas, offloading fan-out from the primary at the cost of extra lag per hop.

In our National Bank of India platform the core ledger is deliberately single-primary because money cannot tolerate conflicting writes, so all balance updates go to one writable node and reporting reads are routed round-robin across replicas. For the far region I use a cascading replica that streams from a nearby replica rather than the primary, which keeps the primary from being overwhelmed by many direct standbys. I only consider active-active when multi-region low-latency writes are a hard requirement and the data model genuinely tolerates conflicts, and even then I partition writes by region to avoid clashes. The line I remember is: single-primary for most workloads, cascading to relieve fan-out, and active-active only when multi-region writes are mandatory and conflict resolution is acceptable.
